articles.fullContent: Anthropic正在从让Claude编写代码转向帮助开发者决定何时可以发布该代码。 周一，这家新近上市的人工智能公司宣布推出Claude Ship，这是一套用于自动化代码审查、修复和常规代码变更批准的人工智能代理。 后者是这套新工具中更有趣的部分，因为在此之前，AI编码工具就已经提供了代码审查功能。 Claude Ship的显著之处不仅在于它能够审核拟议的代码变更，并识别和解决问题，而且它还包含一个代理，该代理可以根据开发团队制定的策略自动批准代码变更。 此次发布正值人工智能编码代理日益具备生成大量代码的能力，导致在代码变更上线前审查和批准代码变更方面出现瓶颈。 使用Claude Ship，其理念是将开发过程中更多的工作自动化，本质上是将审批权限委派给AI代理本身。 “大多数团队都希望由专人来批准每一处变更，当人们亲自编写每一行代码时，这样做很容易跟上进度。 但现在很多开发人员都使用代理进行开发。”该公司的一篇博客文章解释道。 “在Claude Code团队中，Claude编写了我们的大部分代码，我们希望PR之后的所有工作也能同样快速推进。” Claude Ship正在推出测试版，让早期采用者能够使用它来审核拉取请求（PR），然后决定哪些内容已准备好合并。 新产品包括已正式发布的代码评审功能，以及目前处于测试阶段的两个新代理：PR Steward和Claude Approvals。 PR Steward专注于解决CI检查失败、合并冲突以及代码评审反馈等问题。 它还会在每次推送后发表评论，说明更改了哪些内容，以及在需要时如何回滚。 然后，Claude Approvals 会应用团队以文件形式写入代码仓库的审批策略。 此审批流程可以纳入各种信号，包括代码审查结果或公司自己的分类器，以及以自然语言撰写的政策。 由于该产品仍处于测试阶段，Anthropic建议首先以“仅观察”模式运行审批功能。 团队还可以选择仅从一个代码仓库开始，并设置每月支出限额，以便更好地控制该流程。 Anthropic表示，团队仍将掌控Claude Ship的运行位置、要使用的审核设置（例如 快速、标准或深度），以及哪些变更应上报给人工进行决策。 Claude Ship正在面向GitHub上的代码仓库推出Claude Team和Enterprise套餐。 代码审核已正式上线，而 PR Steward 和 Claude Approvals 仍处于测试阶段。 当您通过我们文章中的链接购买时，我们可能会赚取一小笔佣金。 这不会影响我们的编辑独立性。 一家初创公司在印度起诉苹果，原因是“轻点分享”联系人功能 Jagmeet Singh
articles.originalSummary: As AI-generated code piles up, Anthropic's new developer tools aim to eliminate another bottleneck by letting agents handle routine approvals.

articles.fullContent: Richpanel 使用 GPT‑6 Astra 和 GPT‑6。1 Sol 为其 AI 客服专员提供工具和流程，并使用 GPT‑6 Luna 进行对话。 除了知道如何回应客户的请求外，AI 支持专员还需要能够执行解决方案。 为此，他们需要能够使用合适的工具和说明。 据 Richpanel 首席执行官 Amit RG 介绍，人工客服代表在为客户提供服务时可能会使用 20 或 30 种工具，而他们遵循的流程可能从未被记录下来。 Richpanel ⁠（在新窗口中打开）使用OpenAI模型解决了这个问题，既可以设置AI客服专员采取行动和处理客户对话所需的工具，也可以设置所需的程序。 “智能不再是瓶颈。 而是围绕它的所有东西。 “部署支持代理通常需要一名前线部署工程师将代理连接到客户的系统，并确定其工作方式。 Amit发现许多公司没有多余的工程师，于是他问自己：“如果前线部署的工程师本身就是一名AI代理呢？” 于是，Richpanel 打造了这个产品：一个负责处理代理设置的 AI 管理员。 客户开始称之为 Boss AI。 它编写程序，并定义 Richpanel 的一线支持专员、Copilot 和质量保证专员如何调用他们所需的工具。 Richpanel 使用 GPT‑6 Astra 和 GPT‑6. 1 Sol for Boss AI，在构建其他客服代表将遵循的工具和程序时，优先考虑准确性。 Richpanel 设计的一线客服代表能够处理数十万次对话，因此每次互动的成本成为模型选择的一个重要考量因素。 它使用 GPT‑6 Luna 和其他 OpenAI 模型来完成这项工作。 Amit 表示，Richpanel 对其 Copilot 和质量保证客服代表也采取了同样的方法。 “关键在于成本和智能之间的平衡。”Amit 表示。 Richpanel 的客户可能已经在使用低成本的外包支持服务。 与这一起点相比，实现运营自动化必须具有财务意义。 Amit认为，OpenAI提供了能够处理长上下文和更长任务的模型，同时保持了成本效益。 Richpanel 可以使用更深入的推理来培训其客服专员，并使用更经济的模型来开展后续的对话。 在2026年10月的采访中，Amit表示，Richpanel在过去六个月内完成了约300次AI客户支持部署。

articles.fullContent: 人工智能投资初创公司Supertake有一个有趣的前提：如果您的市场“观点”可以让您赚钱，而您又不必亲自挑选股票，那会怎么样？ 该服务让人们能够利用尖端人工智能模型和交易代理，将自己的想法转化为真正的投资组合。 如今，该公司已筹集了2000万美元的种子轮融资，以发展其业务。 本轮融资由风险投资公司Adjacent（Nico Wittenborn）领投，Coinbase Ventures和Union Square Ventures（USV）参与投资。 众多天使投资人也参与其中，包括目前担任Meta Superintelligence Labs产品总监的Nat Friedman、Vercel首席执行官Guillermo Rauch、知名产品经理Nikita Bier、投资人Scott Belsky，以及前Coinbase高管、现任Y Combinator客座合伙人的Nemil Dalal。 Michael Mignano最初是在USV孵化这家初创企业的。 他是播客平台Anchor的联合创始人兼前首席执行官，Spotify于2019年以超过1.5亿美元的价格收购了该平台。 在担任Spotify播客业务“谈话主管”数年后，他以风险合伙人的身份加入Lightspeed团队，投资Suno和Granola等人工智能公司。 他还共同创立了人工智能教育初创公司Oboe，并于4月加入USV担任普通合伙人。 “我们真心相信，有机会让投资更加民主化……让每个人都能根据自己的见解、信念和想法进行投资。”Mignano 表示。 虽然他将继续担任创始人兼执行董事长，但他现在已引入一支团队来负责公司的日常运营。 团队成员包括联合创始人Lincoln Murr（首席执行官）和John Peterson（首席技术官）。 两人均来自Coinbase，Mignano指出，他们在Coinbase担任人工智能产品和工程负责人，主导了Coinbase顾问、Coinbase for agents、代理钱包等产品的发布。 这家初创公司是在人工智能继续进军金融服务领域之际成立的，但要让人工智能接管人们的实际投资，则需要一个新的信任水平。 鉴于尖端人工智能模型近期的改进，Supertake押注人们最终将愿意迈出这一步。 目前，Supertake与Coinbase和Robinhood合作，该公司打算随着时间的推移将业务扩展到更多经纪商。 其理念是，您可以以通俗易懂的自然语言阐述您对世界将如何变化的看法，Supertake 的人工智能将与您反复互动，将这一想法转化为可投资的“观点”。 在幕后，这家初创公司正在利用尖端人工智能技术和工具，并结合其自有专有软件来指导和限制人工智能的运作范围。 Supertake 网站上的排行榜会跟踪用户的想法，这样，其他认同这些想法的人就可以与他们一起投资。 例如，排行榜上目前有一个...

articles.fullContent: 一款开源运行时，可帮助运维人员保护正在运行的 Linux 系统，无需等待补丁或重启OpenAI 和思科正在推出 Shirudo，这是一款开源运行时，可帮助团队在推出补丁的同时保护 Linux 系统。 在一次受控测试中（在新窗口中打开） ，由 Codex 生成的防护机制阻止了针对正在运行的 Elasticsearch 服务的 Java4Shell 漏洞利用尝试，且无需重启。 我们诚邀整个行业的开发者、安全研究人员和基础设施运营商共同参与，帮助进一步推进该项目的发展。 该项目汇集了OpenAI的前沿人工智能、安全和基础设施研究以及思科的基础设施和安全专长，以帮助保护人们每天依赖的系统。 测试和部署补丁仍可能需要数天或数周的时间。 与此同时，保护服务可能具有挑战性，因为漏洞利用和合法请求可能依赖于相同的Linux操作。 完全阻止该操作可能会使服务离线。 Shirudo（日语意为“盾牌”）旨在帮助安全团队应对这种权衡。 团队可以测试一种名为“盾”的临时防护措施是否能够阻止暴露漏洞的行为，同时允许合法请求通过。 一旦操作员批准了防护，就可以在服务继续运行的同时进行部署。 Shirudo 使用 eBPF，这是一种 Linux 技术，允许小型程序在操作系统内的特定点运行。 这使得观察可疑活动并对正在运行的系统应用有针对性的安全保护成为可能。 Guardian 代理如何使用 eBPF 观察和保护正在运行的系统。 OpenAI 和思科正在围绕四项核心功能设计 Shirudo：实时保护：eBPF 屏蔽功能可以在不重启系统的情况下阻止易受攻击的代码路径。 安全团队可以在实施拟议的防护之前，先监测该防护会对应用程序产生怎样的影响。 以机器速度进行防御：OpenAI 和思科正在设计 Shirudo，旨在为代理提供可编程控制功能，以便调查漏洞、开发有针对性的防护措施，并验证其针对漏洞利用和实际工作负载的有效性。 安全团队控制部署的内容。 可信部署：Shield 在加载前经过加密签名和验证。 Linux 的 eBPF 验证器根据其安全规则检查 eBPF 程序，而内核安全控制则限制未经授权的更改。 硬件支持的验证：Shirudo 使用可信平台模块 (TPM) 来支持加载或移除保护的可验证记录。 运营商可以使用这些证据来检查系统是否符合其安全要求。
articles.originalSummary: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo, an open-source runtime for Linux. It helps teams protect running systems while they roll out patches.

articles.fullContent: 从远处看，现代人工智能的构建方式似乎与过去几十年中软件的构建方式相似：使用一套多样化的技术来针对特定的功能。 确实有各种各样的方法，但它们大多不是从零开始设计，而是利用来自一个更简单、更难解释的过程的智能：在一个非常庞大的数据语料库上训练一个压缩器（或等效地（在新窗口中打开） ，预测器）。 1 我认为，跟踪训练更好压缩器的进展速度是理解人工智能发展轨迹的关键。 在本文中，我主张将困惑度（或等效的交叉熵损失）确立为一种指标，用于在模型开发者之间进行比较，并为共同的安全标准提供参考。 作为第一步，我将让OpenAI的预训练进展更加透明。 我们对发布内部困惑度测量结果进行了慎重考虑；这样做会让竞争对手更清楚地了解我们的立场，但与在整个行业建立共同的（在新窗口中打开）安全措施的紧迫性相比，这种顾虑显得微不足道。 我们OpenAI希望此举能成为迈向为未来的步伐控制工作建立共同科学基础的一步。 对人工智能发展的看法，一种简单但本质上具有启发性的观点是：首先，人们构建一台大型计算机，然后使用它在一个大型非结构化数据集上对一个模型（压缩器）进行预训练，接着在不同的语境中应用各种技术——如提示、微调或强化学习——以激发该模型的潜在能力。 算法的进步可能会模糊训练阶段之间的界限，但我们仍然可以将人工智能的创造（我之前称之为“外星人的思维”）与随后有针对性的诱导区分开来，因为人工智能具有难以预测的涌现能力。 多年来，我们衡量这一关键“智能基质”进展的主要方式一直保持着显著的稳定性——我们一直在跟踪模型在留出数据集上的困惑度。 2 , 3困惑度衡量的是模型平均预测下一个token的准确性；困惑度越低，预测越准确。 本文开头展示的图表显示了从 GPT-3 开始，这一指标在我们模型中的演变情况。5. 主要通过这一指标来描述的模型能力范围令人惊叹。 GPT-2 在旧数据集上树立了新的困惑度最高水平 4 ，可以说是有史以来第一个能够持续生成连贯文本段落的模型。 下一个重大飞跃是 GPT-3，它能够在给定任务的几个示例的情况下进行上下文学习。 GPT-3.5 在我们当前的主要评估数据集上的对数困惑度约为 0.99，能够进行流利的对话，并构成了最初的 ChatGPT 的基础。GPT-4 的对数困惑度约为 0.

articles.fullContent: Hebbia 在 GPT‑6 Astra 的测试中看到了金融研究方面的收益。 在 Hebbia 的测试中，领先于表现最佳的替代方案的百分点数。 在 Hebbia 的测试中，与问题相关的引用摘录的百分比。 Hebbia 测试中满足适用呈现要求的百分比。 在演示文稿要求方面，领先于所测试的最佳替代方案的百分点数。 在向客户推荐收购之前，银行家需要弄清财务报表、客户合同和管理层演示文稿。 Hebbia 的 Matrix 有助于整合这些研究，将答案与背后的文件联系起来。 Hebbia 测试了 OpenAI 的 GPT‑6 Astra，以改进这项工作的两个方面：找到问题所需的来源，并根据银行家的简要说明制作演示文稿。 具体运作方式可能是这样的：一位银行家正在帮助客户评估对一家工业软件公司的战略收购，需要审核大约 2000 个文件。 是什么让其收入具有可持续性？ 它与同行相比如何？ 在Hebbia的假设示例中，银行家可以将数据室加载到Matrix中，并在引用的单元格中查看客户集中度、合同条款和流失率。 Matrix可以引入同行备案和行业新闻，帮助制定交易论证，然后将该研究转化为公司的模板中的尽职调查摘要和估值演示文稿。 在该工作流程中，GPT‑6 Astra 会选择文件或 Matrix 单元格来支持答案，然后将分析转换为遵循用户结构和指南的原生 PowerPoint 幻灯片。 “可追溯性对我们的用户来说非常重要，因为他们要根据 AI 实际给出的结果来做出价值数百万美元的决策，”Kavita 表示。 “引用有助于实现可追溯性，并让用户确信人工智能找到了正确的答案。” 在 Hebbia 的测试中，GPT‑6 Astra 将更广泛的来源覆盖范围与高度相关的引用相结合。它获得了 13 分。 在引用所需类型的来源方面，比测试的最佳替代方案高出6个百分点，而其引用的摘录中有99.5%与问题相关。 Hebbia 于 2026 年 8 月至 9 月测试了一个预发布版本，对每个模型使用了相同的金融研究案例和评分标准。 领域专家根据源文档撰写或审核了标准。

articles.fullContent: 我们如何应对蒸馏的安全风险，以及我们在加强整个行业的安全保障方面所吸取的经验教训。 随着前沿人工智能模型的能力不断增强，保障措施在如何负责任地使用这些模型方面发挥着越来越重要的作用。 对抗性蒸馏为不法分子在没有适当保障措施的情况下复制这些能力开辟了一条途径。 行为者可能会在未经授权的情况下使用前沿模型的输出，来训练另一个具有类似功能的模型，然后将其部署，而没有提供同等水平的保护。 例如，攻击者可能会提炼出一个模型的网络能力，并使用由此产生的模型来帮助实施网络攻击，而原始模型本会拒绝协助此类攻击，或者其安全防护措施本会阻止此类攻击。 我们将分享OpenAI如何检测和阻止对抗性蒸馏，我们如何加强对模型受保护推理的保护，以及我们学到了哪些可以帮助加强整个行业的防御措施的经验。 我们处理对抗性蒸馏的方法将对抗性测试、模型训练、分类器和API级保护与对有组织地提取模型能力的企图的调查相结合。 这些更新后的保障措施与我们在生物学和网络安全领域所采用的措施更加一致。 我们特别重视防止攻击者提取我们模型的受保护推理：即模型在努力得出答案的过程中在内部生成的中间步骤，称为其“思维链”。 这些痕迹可能包含最终答案中未提及的信息，因此它们对于另一个模型来说是特别有价值的训练数据。 我们在 GPT‑6 中加强了针对受保护推理提取的防御。2 Astra 和 GPT‑6。2 Sol。在一次使用强大自动化红队的内部自适应评估中，我们测试了攻击者是否能够恢复模型在回答先前提示时生成的受保护推理。 平均攻击成功率从针对具有原始安全防护措施的 GPT‑6 Astra 的 54. 0% 下降到针对具有更新版安全防护措施的 GPT‑6. 2 Astra（采用更新后的安全措施）的攻击成功率降至 0.2%。 蒸馏是一种常见的机器学习技术，其中一个模型从另一个模型产生的数据中学习。 例如，一个模型可以从另一个模型的答案、其推理或其对哪些答案更好以及为什么更好的判断中学习。 除了知识产权问题外，未经授权的蒸馏还会带来严重的安全风险。 通过对抗性蒸馏，第二个模型可以学习先进的前沿能力，而无需继承规范原始模型如何使用这些能力的保障措施。 在网络安全和生物学等双用途领域，这种担忧尤为明显。 一个帮助防御者发现软件漏洞的模型也可能帮助攻击者利用这些漏洞；一个协助生物学研究的模型也可能帮助某人开发有害病原体。 如果将此类能力转移到具有较弱保障措施的模型，该模型可能会提供原始模型会拒绝或原始保障措施会阻止的帮助。 我们的模型可帮助用户完成编码和防御性网络安全任务。 在许多此类良性输出上进行训练的第二个模型可能会学到同样适用于进攻性网络安全任务的技能。

articles.rawFullText: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work. It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development. And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement. METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research. In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance. Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.” Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite. Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.  Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category. But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.” Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].” In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.  In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming. It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

articles.fullContent: 我们由 Codex 提供支持的系统可自动查找和修复性能问题。 代理开发的速度惊人，使得传统的性能工程方法已不再可行。 为了跟上步伐，我们打造了Performance Factory，这是一个自主系统，能够充分利用Codex和我们模型的全部功能，以史无前例的速度发现并修复性能退化问题。 Performance Factory 在云端运行，可自动调查和解决性能问题，使我们能够跟上路线图的宏伟目标。 在 Performance Factory 中，我们的工程师为重复性任务定义工作流，并为执行这些任务的 Codex 代理编写指令。 特别是，当性能警报触发时，回归工作流会打开一个任务。 代理调查速度变慢的情况，将调查结果记录在任务中，并提出解决方案供工程师审核。 部署后，另一名工程师接手同一任务，检查性能是否已恢复到基线水平。 从调查到编写修复方案，再到验证缓解措施，Performance Factory的这个第一个工作流程实现了修复回归的整个过程的自动化。 在短短三个多月的时间里，回归工作流程跟踪了1700多项调查，并找到了600多起个案的根本原因。 这意味着每天有17次自动化调查。 在这里，我们将分享我们如何将Codex的使用发展成为现在的Performance Factory，介绍我们的第一个运行中的工作流程，并分享在生产环境中构建和运行代理工作流程的早期经验教训。 随着我们在更多绩效工作中采用 Codex，我们注意到团队的工作方式有了进步。 我们希望其他服务团队在其他领域采用智能体工作流程时，能够从我们的流程中汲取经验。 软件工作从人工操作发展到与机器合作，再到代理工厂。 1. Codex 之前。在 Codex 之前，工程师需要手动检查指标和日志、比较跟踪、调试运行中的机器并阅读代码，以调查速度变慢的原因。 这项工作非常耗时，而且要弄清楚在哪里查找问题，通常需要对服务有深入的了解。 相关信号很容易被错过。 当我们反复遇到同类问题（例如 ChatGPT 的首个 token 延迟出现回归）时，我们便会构建高级工具（例如 CPU 和分配性能分析器），以便更轻松地进行调查。 随着时间的推移，我们积累了 30 多种性能工具。 2. articles.rawFullText: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack .  You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

articles.rawFullText: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence. Where traditional definitions of trust fall short Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside. Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox. With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned. Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event. Building trust that scales It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest. Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark. The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do. Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions: What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution. Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds. Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step. Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows. Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle. The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. articles.fullContent: 多年来，企业一直将人工智能视为一系列独立的实验。 如今，随着人工智能代理开始进入支撑业务运营的工作流程，这种模式开始显得力不从心。 从孤立的试点转向 AI 代理和自主工作流程的组织正面临着一个更深层次的挑战：重新思考数据、业务流程、治理和人员如何相互配合，将 AI 从一系列工具转变为企业运营模式的一部分。 对于SAP业务人工智能平台生态系统高级副总裁兼全球负责人Thorsten Leiduck来说，这种转变始于将人工智能视为一个企业平台，而不是一系列互不关联的项目。 “人工智能完全依赖于数据基础，”他表示，并认为企业需要一个互联且语义丰富的层来反映其业务，然后才能在各个流程中可靠地部署人工智能。 随着人工智能进入任务关键型工作流程，其利害关系也会发生变化。 他说，对于一些日常应用来说，“80%可能就足够好了”，但在供应链或财务结算等领域，这样的准确率“是一个非常糟糕的结果”。这一基础还决定了哪些人工智能应用值得追求。 Infosys SAP BAIP和SAP AI战略北美区副总裁Satinder Pal Singh将AI代理称为“数字同事”，并建议从三个角度评估潜在用例：影响、可行性和可扩展性。 公司应确定代理可以在哪些方面推动有意义的业务指标，确定其数据和人才是否能够支持该用例，然后确定成功的应用是否可以复制。 “无法扩展的试点项目只是一项实验，”他说。 扩展还会使治理问题更加突出。 明确的政策、访问控制、监控和监督是必要的，以确保代理始终值得信赖并符合业务要求。 “缺乏治理并不会加快人工智能的采用，”Singh 表示。 “它会造成风险积压”，最终可能迫使企业进行更具破坏性的停用和审计。 随着人工智能代理作为数字同事承担更多责任，这些考虑因素将变得更加重要。 两位高管都展望着一个未来，即代理系统协调跨应用程序的工作，而针对具体客户的知识图谱和受管控的数据将成为关键的企业资产。 在Singh看来，长期的机会在于将人工智能从生产力工具转变为“决策合作伙伴”，帮助领导者了解当前情况、预测未来发展并确定应对方式。 本期《商业实验室》由Infosys合作制作。

articles.rawFullText: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model. For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.” That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says. Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit. Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond. This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Infosys. Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace. This episode is produced in partnership with Infosys. Now, the development and democratization of AI tools has the potential to reconfigure how enterprises operate. But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we’re still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI’s value, risk, and the complexity it adds. It’s becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift. Put simply, the technology can’t simply be added into an enterprise’s existing toolkit. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what’s inside and how it’s used. Two words for you: conscious configuration. My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy. Welcome, Thorsten and Satinder. Thorsten Leiduck: Yeah, thank you for having us. Really a pleasure to be here with our valued partner, Infosys. Looking forward to the conversation. Satinder Pal Singh: Hi, Megan. Thanks for inviting for the conversation today. Looking forward to the discussion. Megan: Me too. Thank you both so much for being here. Thorsten, if I could start with you. We know that many senior leaders understand the transformative potential in AI, but they continue to struggle with aspects of its implementation. Many projects remain stuck at a pilot phase, for example. When you speak to clients, what are the biggest obstacles they face when it comes to integrating AI into their tech stack? Thorsten: Yeah. Megan, as you mentioned, AI is on the agenda of every client conversation today, but many customers are really struggling how to convert that interest into an operationalized model and to unlock the value of AI across the enterprise. And the reason is that too many programs start as isolated POCs on different AI technologies and in an inconsistent fragmented data foundation. This creates a lot of duplication, inconsistent performance, and no clear path to scale. At the same time, leaders are highly concerned about security, observability, reliability of agents, and some ethical implications when those get deployed. This is also shown in some studies. For example, BCG has launched a report, which shows that 74% of the organizations are stuck in pilot mode with no plan to scale. And in an Anthropic survey, data said that 42% are really struggling with getting access to the data and the quality to really, basically, scale the entire AI capabilities across the organization. The path forward is really to treat AI not just as a project, but more holistically, as an enterprise platform, one that really consistently connects an unified data layer with the process context of the applications, and then embed AI capabilities governed across the entire life cycle. And to make this real, we in SAP launched the SAP autonomous enterprise framework, so organizations can move from pilots to scaled outcomes. Megan: Yeah, really, to provide that support. And, Satinder, would you agree, why is it that we’re seeing enterprises get a touch of almost AI paralysis here? What’s the mindset shift that needs to happen and, perhaps, why is this something organizations need to be thinking about now, as well? Satinder: Absolutely, Megan. And, if anything, the picture sharpens when you look at, specifically, at agentic AI. Infosys and HFS research surveyed over 500 global 2,000 enterprises and found only 14% have successfully scaled AI. Eighty-six percent remain in early exploration, proof of concept, or fragmented pilot phases. For a technology at the top of every boardroom agenda for two years, that’s a striking failure rate. And at the core of that 86% is what I would describe as AI as a department trap. What happens is that an organization creates an AI team or a center of excellence and walls it off from business. That team builds technically excellent pilots the business doesn’t recognize itself in, and you end up with AI solutions searching for problems, rather than the other way around. Mindset shift is clear. Move from treating AI as a technology initiative to treating it as an operating model transformation. AI stops being something IT does for business and starts being something the whole organization does together. Every function, every workflow, embedded from the start. And what makes this a now problem? Early movers are building an advantage. You cannot close by buying the same platform later. Eighteen months of agent behavior data, calibrated knowledge graph, workforce that has genuinely internalized AI, that is a structural advantage that compounds. Infosys Knowledge Institute AI Maturity Index shows that only 8% of the companies qualify as AI native today, yet they achieve four times the revenue contribution from the AI versus laggards. If you’re not building AI today, you’re not standing still, you’re falling behind at an accelerating rate. Megan: Right. There’s a real polarization there, isn’t there, between the front-runners and the laggards, as you say. As we shift from pilot to scaled-up applications, perhaps the first step is evaluating when AI is the right tool. AI has quickly become the default solution within many enterprises. Is there a tendency to use it as a bit of a blunt instrument, nowadays, Thorsten? At the outset, how can senior leaders better evaluate what use cases are worthy of their time and investment, in order to strip out some of that later complexity? Thorsten: Yeah, I think, Megan, what everybody needs to be aware is adopting and rolling out AI across an organization is as much a change management journey as it’s a technology rollout. Now, when you have this in mind, it makes absolutely sense to put AI in front as many teams as possible, because you want to build formality, and spark ideas, and also people should see the benefit of AI in an organization. When you think about travel assistance, meeting summaries via Copilot, or AI-enabled workflows, increase the productivity, everybody feels this in their real job, in their real daily business. And, obviously, this creates creativity and also provides the organization from a bottom-up perspective with some innovation scale. Now, however, as majority grows, the conversation, and this is also what we discuss with many of the leaders, and our clients, shifts more to economics and governance. Things like token costs, model performance, security, and accountability become much more relevant. And when you then take the approach and think about AI agents as digital workers that execute specific tasks within a business process, then this means, from an AI perspective, not every task justifies nation. In some cases, human effort remains more economical or effective. The smart approach, and that’s what we really recommend to our clients, is to start with a defined, maybe small set of high-value use cases with defined success metrics upfront. So, for example, such as cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, or cost of per transaction, or top line improvement, and then scale what works. Those use cases can be tied to a line of business domains or industry scenarios. And then, what we are doing from an SAP perspective, together with Infosys, we really help customers to be successful. We provide, as part of our autonomous suite, the according domain assistance, which really run business processes end-to-end and which deliver find ROIs for single end-to-end business process steps. And then, last but not least, in many scenarios, I think, which has been very common pattern in particular around large industry AI use cases, is a joint approach, and we do this with partners like Infosys, but also customers around forward deployed engineering, so that you really define very closely the AI-specific use case with the defined outcomes together with the customer, and deliver this as the initial projects. And then, ideally, scale this to other customers and take it back like a best practice, which can be rolled out to other organizations, as well. Megan: Right. It’s been really clear, isn’t it, on what you’re looking to achieve and what’s worth your time, as I say. And what would your advice, Satinder, be here, on refining an AI strategy to ensure organizations can focus on those areas, where AI can deliver the highest returns? Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten’s framing of AI agents as digital coworkers forces a precision that agentic AI strategy language often lacks. When you ask which digital coworkers do we need and where do they deliver the most value, the answer starts to become clearer right from the first step. At Infosys, through our Topaz AI-first framework, we push clients through the three lenses simultaneously. The first one is impact. Where does deploying an agent move the numbers that matter? Revenue, cost, working capital risk. We have built a library of over 300 enterprise use cases across industries, so we never begin from a blank page. The second is feasibility. Given your data foundation platform and talent today, which high-impact use cases can you actually execute? Feasibility determines your sequence. The high-impact use case on a broken data foundation is not viable. When the foundation is right, the results are dramatic. One Infosys engagement cut complex SAP-specification documents from 86 person hours to 6, a 92% reduction. Third is scalability. Once you have proven a use case with clear ROI metrics, cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, cost per transaction, what’s the architecture that lets you replicate it? A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment. My practical advice: treat your AI portfolio like an investment portfolio, quick wins that fund the program, medium-term bets, one or two bold, long-term positions that balance keep stakeholders engaged at every stage and not just in year three. Megan: That’s such a useful framework for people to use there. And given the urgency here, Thorsten, how can organizations approach and manage AI in a more structured, efficient way? To start with, what are the fundamentals that some organizations perhaps miss at the moment? I know Infosys and SAP talk about platform and data, then AI, for example. Thorsten: Yeah, Megan, I think the fundamental, which many organizations are overlooking, is data and the data is a foundation for AI. Because, at the end, without the data structures and the ability to access the right information at the right time and basically bringing different kind of structured, unstructured data sources together, in a meaningful governed and semantic way, there will be no successful AI. AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation. And I think this is often overlooked, and that’s why I said when you start POCs in different organization, or different parts of the organization with different technologies, it’s very hard to establish an end-to-end consistent model on the data side, as well as on the AI side. One of the key goals companies need to achieve is, and that’s why we really talk about you need to start with data first and the platform first, is to establish and semantically-rich connected data layer that really reflects your business, so that the agents are really grounded in the company’s reality and not just in generic patterns. And then, I think, the second element that’s important is accuracy. In the enterprise context, it really matters. For example, what might pass in a consumer setting, where you have 80% accuracy, and even in a workforce environment where you build PowerPoints or you do email drafts, which you then, with a human in the loop, optimize, 80% might be good enough. But, when you really think about mission-critical or business-critical processes in the supply chain, or closing the books, 80% is a very terrible result. The stakes are much too high and you need to have much more accuracy. And that’s why it’s important that you have business process logic and industry context embedded into the data and the models which build the foundation, if you will, the backbone for every AI and, obviously, for the data in the ERP and the line of business system. And then, last but not least, the other critical element, and you see this obviously in the news with all the agents going rogue, are governance, compliance, and security. Very critical in an enterprise context. You need to set clear policies, access controls. You need to have monitoring ability, capabilities, to really make sure that what then the AI agenda capabilities or agents are executing is fully aligned, is trustworthy, and scalable. Megan: Right. Which is quite a lot of things for organizations to be thinking about. Satinder, how do SAP and Infosys work with organizations to streamline some of these processes, perhaps and make unlocking AI’s capability a little bit easier? Satinder: Megan, I think at the onset, I want to acknowledge that, at Infosys, we are uniquely positioned for our relationship with SAP, because we are a customer to SAP, as well as one of their key global suppliers. And the way SAP and Infosys work together is designed around the architecture Thorsten described, that defines a coherent partnership. SAP brings the platform foundation, business data cloud for the semantically-rich enterprise, generative AI hub for governed LLMXs, and agent hub for the lifecycle governance, enterprise grade from day one. Infosys brings implementation depth, industry context, and use case accelerators. Through Infosys Topaz, we have built over 50 pre-configured AI use cases on Business AI Platform, production-ready configurations deployable without building from scratch. We co-develop use cases within SAP’s industry AI engagement with clear customer-specific FTE metrics. That shared accountability for results is different from a typical implementation engagement. In practice, one global S/4HANA transformation program used AI-assisted delivery tooling to complete over 480 RICEF objects in five months, a pace conventional delivery would not sustain. In another account, an AI-powered platform auto-classifies over 120,000 SAP incidents monthly, with zero analyst charge. The combined effect time to value drops from 12 to 18 months, down to four to six months. What I would emphasize is change management damage. Technology is increasingly deployable, and Thorsten also spoke about it earlier. What’s hard is helping an organization internalize that their agents are digital coworkers, not automations . That mindset shift is 70% of the implementation challenge that platform cannot solve alone, and Infosys and SAP run joint adoption programs addressing both the dimensions in parallel. Megan: Fantastic. Some great real-world examples there, as well. Thorsten, can you tell us a little bit more about SAP’s Business AI Platform, or BAIP, in particular? How does that work and what sets it apart from other platforms? Thorsten: Yeah, so SAP Business AI Platform, if you will, is the foundation for our SAP autonomous enterprise framework, which really consists of a unified user interface and is enabled as an agentic orchestration layer, which we call Joule. And you have the autonomous read with all the applications, and then you have the Business AI Platform, which powers the other capabilities, and is closely connected, and is basically organized around three core pillars. The first one is, really, what we call build. What it means is you provide the respective intent-based development tools, so that customer, or partners like Infosys, can really create and development agents, applications and workflows using best-in-class tools and model to extend SAP’s own assistant, or customizing those, or really building own agents as needed. Complimenting what Satinder said, it’s really critical for us that we have a thriving ecosystem, who is innovative, and is building innovations, and is complementing our own SAP agentic portfolio. We are focusing on specific areas on the domains, from a line of business industry perspective, where we deliver assistance as part of our organization, but to really then customize them from a last mile execution from really complimenting areas which we don’t cover and really driving the innovation towards the customer, our ecosystem is the multiplier force and Infosys is really playing a leading role here with us, together. Second is, and we talked about this, is what we call the contextualize and reason pillar, which is literally as a foundation data, we address with SAP Data Cloud and comprehensive data strategy, where we establish an end-to-end data fabric across partner provider platforms, like Databricks, Snowflakes, where we promote and zero copy access to data. For the customer, this is very important. So, we allow, basically, promote to customers if you have made investments in any of those platforms, reserve those investments and just leverage BDC to connect without moving data around your, for example, Databricks, Snowflake environment to BDC. With this approach, we establish and harmonize semantic data layer, which can then be used for any AI scenario across the entire enterprise, combining different data sources without any disruption. The other key element that’s part of this is the generative AI hub. We have aggregated more than 50 models, language models, including some of our own models into it, in single cockpit, so that customers can access and choose any of those 50 models as part of the generative-AI hub, which is part of the platform. And then, as a key differentiator, we really moved a lot of business semantic and context into the knowledge graph, which then helps to navigate the agents and acts like a nerve, or navigation system, in the company to really provide business-relevant, customer-specific information for the decision making and the execution to any agentic execution framework. And then, we talked about governance, last but not least. This is the third pillar, which is very critical and this is built-in. So, we have, as the third pillar, the SAP agent hub, which is kind of a command center for enterprise-wide AI and agent governments. You can govern SAP agents, you can also govern non-SAP agents, as long as they’re integrating to SAP via A2A. So, the team can really manage, on the customer side, an end-to-end life cycle of agents and features from hire to retire. Megan: Fantastic. That’s a really comprehensive overview. Thank you ever so much. And, Satinder, can you share any examples, perhaps, of how organizations have used SAP Business AI Platform in practice, to improve the ways they’ve used AI? Perhaps, what was the challenge they faced, what did the process look like, and what benefits did they unlock? Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten just explained how powerful a platform Business AI Platform is. And this is decades in working. We also have been using that, and I’ll share two examples from live Infosys engagements, both showing what BIP’s three pillar look like in production. The first is global diversified manufacturer with a large SAP estate. The challenge was month-end close, 80-plus SAP transaction codes, period closed teams working nights and weekends, L1 support absorbing over 300 incidents per month, from close cycle alone. On Business AI Platform, we deployed Topaz Fabric, Infosys’ agentic orchestration platform, with a master agent coordinating five specialist child agents, WBS accrual, revenue recognition, intercompany settlement, master data reconciliation, and SOX audit trail generation. Agents run autonomously, escalating to humans only for genuine exceptions. The result, entire L1.5 support tier eliminated, over 300 monthly incidents handled with zero human touch. The close team redeployed from reactive firefighting to forward-looking financial analysis. Annual savings pipeline exceed $1 million. The second is North American Utility in a S/4HANA transformation. Their challenge was development velocity, complex SAP functional specification documents routinely requiring 80 or more personnel each, a bottleneck throttling the entire program. Using AI native development environment on Business AI Platform with a Claude-powered retrieval system, we reduced those specifications from 86 hours to six, a 92% reduction, validated across 51 SAP task types at 95% accuracy. The architecture is now being replicated across accounts. In both cases, the pattern matches what Thorsten described, governed data foundation, SAP business process context, full agent observability through SAP Agent Hub. That’s the autonomous enterprise running as daily operations, not as a concept. Megan: And those are some really compelling concrete results I think would be really helpful for people to hear. Also, of course, responsible AI, or clear governance frameworks, are a critical component of AI integration, too. And we know that tools like LLMs are rarely developed with compliance built-in. I wonder what’s your advice there, Thorsten, on how to ensure that property governance is embedded into an ERP? Thorsten: Yeah, I mean, Megan, you’re absolutely right. Governance compliance and security are really mission-critical to delivering relevant, reliable, and trustworthy AI at enterprise scale. I mean, it’s important to understand how in public LLM service really works. Many of those services are trained on internet scale data, which means they’re public models. Depending on the provider’s policies and setting, they may retain easier inputs for model improvement, which means if a company provides data back to the model, this company data is in the public domain. For example, pipeline information or forecast information, which is becoming very, very critical, because this exposes your organization, really, at significant risk. So, while then LLMs X are really great, imposes in large volumes of text and other unstructured data, they are less effective with structured tables like in EOP systems, or in business applications, in general, and then they’re lacking, usually, the nuance of business process and logic and context. That’s why a robust governance framework is essential. We talked about the generative AI, how we aggregate those models in a single cockpit. And then, the other element, which we previously touched based on and Satinder mentioned, is always a part of the custom examples is SAP agent hub or, in general, when we talk about the capabilities just in AI lifecycle governance, which really includes agent registry, LMN registries, MCP registry, so a single source of tool for every AI artifact that you can manage identity and access control, so that agents are really variable and that you can really provide the right permissions, in terms of which agents allowed to use access which data, and then agent observability, agent minus, and then also map the agent skills to the organization is very critical. As all of part of this, as I mentioned before, we provide those capabilities really fully embedded into the Business AI Platform to really provide this governance framework out of the box and fully embedded into everything what you do at SAP. Megan: Which is so important, because when organizations are experimenting with, or scaling up multiple AI programs and tools, in some cases, it adds real complexity. I wonder, Satinder, would you add anything on how organizations can have that robust layer of governance built in, even with a pretty complex tech stack? Satinder: We, at Infosys, have our Infosys Knowledge Institute, they run this annual magazine generative AI radar, and it found that 48% of companies had deployed generative AI without a formal governance policy. Nearly half of the enterprises were running AI with no documented framework or oversight, accountability, or compliance. That’s the gap that Thorsten is describing, and it has to be closed proactively before an incident forces a reactive stop or audit far more disruptive than building a governance upfront. What Thorsten has just described in SAP Agent Hub is exactly the platform layer that makes enterprise-wide governance possible and is worth making the overall architecture explicit, because without it, governance is theoretical. The framework I use with clients has three layers that have to work together. The first one is policy, a clear organization-wide AI use policy, what agents can and cannot do autonomously, how data can be used for AI training, disclosure obligations, and accountability for outcomes. This needs legal, compliance, technology teams together with a board level sponsorship. Without that foundation, every deployment becomes an ad hoc governance debate. Second layer is platform. This is where SAP Business AI Platform and, specifically, SAP Agent Hub becomes enterprise control tower. The capabilities Thorsten described, agent LLM, MCP registry as a single source of truth, verifiable agent identities with scoped access trails, agent observability, agent mining for drift detection, these aren’t just governance features. They give leaders real-time visibility across a complex multi-agent landscape. You can see what’s running, what it’s consuming, and whether it’s performing as expected. That’s what turns a complex tech stack from a governance liability to a governance asset. And the last layer is process, the recurring governance rituals, quarterly AI risk reviews, bias audit cycles, model performance reviews against the business KPIs, these structured conversations that keep humans accountable for the agent behavior over time. What organizations consistently discover is that this three-layer structure actually accelerates the deployment. Every new use case has a clear path through approval and a governance architecture to plug into. The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption. It creates a risk backlog that eventually forces a stop and audit movement far more disruptive than building the governance muscle. Megan: That’s such an interesting point. Thank you so much for that. And we’ve covered a lot of ground, so to close with a future forward look, we’ve spoken today about the proliferation of AI tools that are now on the market, many designed to transform enterprise-level operations. I wonder, what do you see on the horizon, Thorsten, that you think could be a real game-changer? Thorsten: I think what we will see very soon, and we talked about this briefly, is that we are heading into a period of sustained, rapid AI adoption, where assistance and agents will operate as digital coworkers. They will be embedded in our organizations like employees today, and they will be embedded into processes as people perform tasks, as we speak. Now, as this happens, the Center of Gravity will shift more and more from a monolithic application layer to an agentic value layer that orchestrates work across systems and across different landscapes, which need to be orchestrated very well. I think what we also will see, and this will be likely, at least in terms of scale, I believe a game-changer, is that the delivery will become industrialized. When you think about agent factories and church services that really design, test, and govern agents at scale, or you can say agentic frameworks at scale, and I think we will see an evolution of commercial models, which are today more consumption-based towards really value and outcome-based agreements, which are then tied to clear business KPIs. On the technology front, I think there’s still so much movement on the LLM landscape, new architectures, training methods. I think we’ll bring down, significantly, the total cost of ownership, while also control and the viability will be improved. I think there’s an awareness which the recent examples in the market show, and then I think the innovation will be playable. And I think the big question is, from that perspective, which role is China going to play in a global context, and also how those models are really embedded. Last but not least, most importantly, even I think ontology and customer-specific knowledge graphs will become first-class assets, and I think this will be the key differentiation in the future, because they will lead in code process, semantics, policies, what Satinder talked about, and data relationships. And they are the blueprint for secure high-performing enterprise agent architectures in the future. Megan: Which is, of course, what we’re aiming for. And how about you, Satinder? What would you flag as a really exciting area of development? Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think what excites me most is the shift from AI as productivity tool to AI as a decision-making partner. The most important evolution Thorsten’s architecture makes possible. For decades, enterprise systems have told us what happened. The next generation helps leader understand what is happening now, what will happen next, what actions to take. The scenario I keep coming back to, a CFO starting a day with an agent that continuously analyzes signals across finance, supply chain, procurement, workforce data, proactively surfacing the three issues that are most likely to impact the quarter, with recommended actions, financial impact quantified. That’s not a dashboard. That’s a fundamentally different decision model. Through Infosys Topaz, we are helping clients move forward an AI-first enterprise, one that can sense, learn, decide, adapt continuously across the different domains. What also excites me is the pace of AI evolution. In past technology waves, constraints were stable. You identify a limitation and architect around it for years. AI is different. Use cases that appear constrained at program start are often resolved before go live. SAP’s prior model transformed structured data reasoning once a clear LLM gap. Decision intelligence is arriving faster than most organization are planning for. The winning strategy is to design for where AI will be 18 months from now, flexible architecture, trusted data foundation, governance that absorbs innovation as it arrives. Organizations that do this compound value at each new generation of capabilities becomes available. So, the next frontier isn’t that AI can do more work. It’s that AI that understands your business well enough to help you make better decision. And that’s where the greatest opportunity for SAP, Infosys, and our clients lies, convergence of systems of record with systems of intelligence. Megan: Fantastic. Certainly, lots on the horizon to look forward to. Thank you both so much for joining us today. That was Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America at SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England. That’s it for this episode of Business Lab. I’m your host, Megan Tatum. I’m a contributing editor and host for Insights, the custom publishing division of MIT Technology Review. articles.fullContent: 这篇文章最初刊登在我们的每周人工智能通讯《The Algorithm》上。 如需第一时间在您的收件箱中收到此类报道，请在此处订阅。 周五，一份要求恢复黄仁勋担任英伟达首席执行官的请愿书开始在社交媒体上流传，到周一，请愿书上列出了一些知名签名人，包括埃隆·马斯克和几位有影响力的英伟达研究人员。 但仔细梳理一下这11.5万多个名字，您就会发现，黄仁勋的支持者中有一个庞大的派系——来自AI模型共享平台Hugging Face的高层，以及风险投资公司Andreessen Horowitz和红杉资本——他们都来自科技界的某个特定群体。 这些名字在开源人工智能的发展中有着既得利益，与ChatGPT或Claude不同，这些模型可以下载并独立于大型科技公司运行。 这种模式的支持者表示，如果将人工智能集中在少数几家实力雄厚的公司手中，其他人就会陷入更加不利的境地（如果不是有这么多开源倡导者同时也是风险投资家，他们会在初创公司能够利用更便宜的人工智能而无需向大型科技公司付费时从中获利，那么这种担忧在左翼人工智能行业批评者中听起来就不会显得格格不入）。 黄仁勋已成为向政策制定者捍卫开源事业的领军人物，以应对人们的担忧，即此类模型没有安全防护措施，并将人工智能的领导地位拱手让给中国，而最强大、最受欢迎的开源模型正是诞生于中国。 他们现在希望这位最有影响力的代言人重返岗位。 但威胁到他（以及英伟达）作为开源人工智能倡导者的信誉的，不仅仅是黄仁勋的婚外情。 一项针对中国使用英伟达芯片的初创企业的新研究，以及美国商务部周一宣布的一项新规定，可能会对该运动的声誉及其技术进步造成打击。 周四，也就是黄辞职的那天，前OpenAI研究员Will DePue在网上发布了研究结果，表明中国的人工智能公司获得英伟达先进的Blackwell芯片的渠道比此前估计的要多得多。 中国被禁止使用英伟达最尖端的芯片，以帮助保护美国在人工智能领域的领先地位。 目前尚不清楚他们是如何获得这些芯片的。 DePue声称，这些结果已得到OpenAI和Anthropic高级研究人员的验证，但独立分析尚未证实这些结果。 （DePue未回复采访请求。 英伟达未立即回应置评请求。 )调查结果并未证实英伟达帮助中国公司获得芯片，而且众所周知，芯片走私这一更广泛的问题早已超出英伟达的控制范围。 但这些调查结果暗示，英伟达可能从中国人工智能初创企业的崛起中获益，而美国公司越来越多地使用这些初创企业的模型，而不是国内的替代产品，这确实让黄仁勋陷入了尴尬的境地。 他一直倡导将开源人工智能作为加强美国技术领先地位的一种方式。 去年12月，他在一次关于帮助美国在与中国的AI竞赛中取胜的演讲中表示：“如果没有开源，初创企业就无法蓬勃发展，大学研究人员就无法开展研究，你就无法教授AI，科学家就无法使用AI。” 这也让黄仁勋复职的希望更加渺茫。

articles.rawFullText: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.  But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.  On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.  But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good. The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

articles.rawFullText: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.  The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option. Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so. But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.   In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

articles.rawFullText: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.  One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .  Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.  Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that. But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something. So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia. But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”
